newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Italy,France,Germany bunch in EMU race - OECD.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy,France,Germany bunch in EMU race - OECD.

text.p: Italy, France and Germany are likely to be neck-in-neck in the race to cut their budget deficits and qualify for monetary union this year, according to forecasts published by the OECD on Thursday.

It forecast all three showing a total public deficit of 3.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, just shy of a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty which calls for deficits to be reduced to three percent of GDP.
The forecasts, which some economists said may already be outdated, had little impact on financial markets.

But economists said the forecasts pointed towards a broad membership of monetary union, rather than the narrow one sought by Germany, which is trying to cut its deficit to 3.0 percent of GDP to ensure a strict reading of Maastricht criteria.

"It's not bad enough to provoke thoughts of delay (in economic and monetary union)," Sonja Gibbs, economist at Nomura in London, said. "On the face of it, if it has any impact at all, it is definitely broad EMU friendly."

The Organisation for Economic and Co-operation and Development also forecast in its half-year economic outlook that Germany and France would continue to cut their deficits in 1998, to 2.7 and 3.0 percent of GDP respectively.
But Italy's deficit/GDP ratio was seen rising sharply to 3.8 percent in 1998.
European Union countries are due to decide in April/May 1998 which countries qualify to join a single currency at its launch on the basis of economic and fiscal performance in 1997.

Officials have recently been stressing the fact the deficit cuts must be sustainable, in what some see as a warning to Italy that even if it meets Maastricht this year it may still be excluded if it cannot stay the course in future years.
But the OECD did not take account of any new budget measures -- a factor which may be particularly significant for Italy which has promised a three-year plan to reduce its debt and public deficit.
"I think (the forecasts) are quite bullish for Italy," UBS economist Darren Williams said.

He noted the OECD's Italian short-term interest rate forecasts, at 7.3 percent this year and 6.4 percent next year, did not take account of a likely fall in rates as European rates converge ahead of monetary union.
Any interest rate fall would reduce significantly debt service changes -- the main factor in Italy's deficit.
The OECD also forecast Spain and Portugal would meet the Maastricht budget deficit criterion.
It saw Spain's deficit/GDP ratio at 3.0 percent in 1997 and 2.6 percent in 1998, and Portugal's at 2.9 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
Spain's determination to join EMU at the start in 1999 has been a key factor in convincing Italy it, too, should be included when the single currency is launched.

Economists said however that more important than the deficit figures were political developments in Europe, particularly in France where the new Socialist-led government has been fighting to end austerity in the EU.

France has said it wants Italy and Spain to join EMU at the start, that there should be a flexible interpretion of the Maastricht treaty, and that it will not impose new austerity just to cut the deficit/GDP ratio to exactly 3.0 percent.
"The ball is still in France's court," Gibbs said.
